result.markdown: --- title: "Does a protective skin microbiome save the population?" subtitle: "Building biological realism one step at a time" engine: julia --- ## The question and the method Amphibians can be treated with skin bacteria that inhibit the chytrid fungi *Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis* (Bd) and *B. salamandrivorans* (Bsal). Would that protect a population? The answer a model gives depends on how much biology is in it. This vignette makes that dependence visible. For each of three host–pathogen systems it: 1. starts from the **simplest model** of the host and the pathogen; 2. adds the **biology of the host and pathogen** one piece at a time, with no treatment; 3. adds the **biology of the treatment** one piece at a time; 4. after every step, records the same two outcomes: the population **without treatment**, and the population under one fixed **reference treatment**; 5. ends with **chance**: the last model of each part is run again with whole animals and random events, many times over. Every step keeps everything before it and changes one thing. Most steps add a piece of biology; a few replace a placeholder with a more realistic version of the same piece (blocking infection with the effect seen in trials, a fixed "treated" state with bacteria that decline). The equations at the start of each part list the settings every step uses. The final sections measure how much each addition moved the answer, and check with a factorial design whether the effect of one piece of realism depends on the others. A [second vignette](../02_nested_model/02_nested_model.md) repeats the exercise in a single nested model, where every combination of pieces can be compared like for like. | Part | System | Simplest model | |---|---|---| | A | Bsal in fire salamanders | susceptible and infectious adults | | B | Bd in common toads | Mitchell et al. (2008) pond model | | C | Bd in frogs | Briggs et al. (2010) load model | ::: {.callout-important} The published models (Schmidt et al. 2017, Mitchell et al. 2008, Briggs et al. 2010) are reproduced from their papers. Everything added to them is new work in this package and **is not a published result**. Values taken from experiments are read from the package's parameter compendium and are named where they are used. All other added values (efficacy, coverage, spread, exposure windows, clearance) are illustrative: they show what the model does, not what a real treatment would achieve. ::: ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Chytridiomycosis, Plots, Printf using Distributions: LogNormal, quantile using Random: Xoshiro, shuffle default(linewidth = 2, size = (720, 380), legendfontsize = 8, guidefontsize = 9, titlefontsize = 10, left_margin = 4Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 4Plots.mm) include("../diagram.jl") T(; kw...) = MicrobiomeTreatment(; kw...) # One row per step, filled in as we go. `untreated` and `treated` are the two outcomes; # NaN where one does not apply. ladder = NamedTuple[] function step!(system, phase, added, untreated, treated, note) n = count(r -> r.system == system, ladder) push!(ladder, (; system, n, phase, added, untreated, treated, note)) return (step = n, untreated = round(untreated, digits = 3), treated = round(treated, digits = 3)) end function ladder_plot(system, xlabel) rows = filter(r -> r.system == system, ladder) k = length(rows) labels = ["$(r.n). $(r.added)" for r in rows] z(x) = isnan(x) ? 0.0 : x bar((1:k) .- 0.2, [z(r.untreated) for r in rows]; orientation = :h, bar_width = 0.38, label = "no treatment", color = :gray70, yticks = (1:k, labels), yflip = true, xlabel, xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1, size = (840, 80 + 36k), left_margin = 6Plots.mm, legend = :outertop, legend_column = 2) bar!((1:k) .+ 0.2, [z(r.treated) for r in rows]; orientation = :h, bar_width = 0.38, label = "with treatment", color = :steelblue) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ladder_plot (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ## Part A. Bsal in fire salamanders The outcome in Part A is the **mean number of adults over the ten years after Bsal arrives, as a fraction of carrying capacity**. The reference treatment is: every adult treated once, on the day Bsal arrives, with bacteria that block 99% of infections for life. ### Host and pathogen #### Step 0. Susceptible and infectious adults The simplest model: an adult is susceptible or infectious, infection passes by contact, and infectious animals die of the disease. This is the model of Schmidt et al. (2017) with its latent period made negligibly short. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} p = SchmidtParameters(:schmidt2017) p_si = Chytridiomycosis.with(p; e = 5000.0) # latent period under two hours block = T(efficacy = 0.99) sli(q, tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticSLIProblem(q, tr; kw...)) u0, t0 = sli(p_si, T()), sli(p_si, block; coverage = 1.0) @printf("R0 = %.1f\n", basic_reproduction_number(p_si)) step!("Bsal", "host", "susceptible and infectious adults", u0.mean_hosts, t0.mean_hosts, "collapse; treated adults live but are not replaced") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R0 = 24.8 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (step = 0, untreated = 0.003, treated = 0.338) ``` ::: ::: #### Step 1. A latent period Infected animals are not infectious at once (Schmidt et al. 2017, as published). ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} u1, t1 = sli(p, T()), sli(p, block; coverage = 1.0) @printf("R0 = %.1f\n", basic_reproduction_number(p)) step!("Bsal", "host", "+ latent period (Schmidt 2017)", u1.mean_hosts, t1.mean_hosts, "almost no change: a one-day delay against a one-week illness") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R0 = 24.8 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (step = 1, untreated = 0.004, treated = 0.338) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plot(u1.t, u1.hosts ./ p.K; label = "no treatment", xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)") plot!(t1.t, t1.hosts ./ p.K; label = "all adults treated once") plot!(t1.t, t1.treated ./ p.K; label = "of which still treated", linestyle = :dash) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Treated adults survive, but the population still declines: recruits are born untreated and Bsal is still circulating. #### Step 2. A larval stage Salamanders have aquatic larvae. Here they are added as a stage that Bsal does not infect. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} clean_larvae = BsalLarvalStage(carry_over = 0.0) lar(st, tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticLarvalProblem(p, st, tr; kw...)) u2, t2 = lar(clean_larvae, T()), lar(clean_larvae, block; coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", "host", "+ larval stage, not infected", u2.mean_adults, t2.mean_adults, "untreated population no longer vanishes: larvae are a refuge") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (step = 2, untreated = 0.044, treated = 0.336) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plot(u1.t, max.(u1.hosts ./ p.K, 1e-12); yscale = :log10, label = "adults only (step 1)", xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K), no treatment", legend = :bottomright) plot!(u2.t, u2.adults ./ p.K; label = "with a larval stage (step 2)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Larvae already in the water metamorphose after the adult epidemic has burnt out. The near-extinction in the adults-only model was partly a result of having no other stage. #### Step 3. Larvae can be infected Fire salamander larvae can be infected experimentally without showing disease, and half carried the infection through metamorphosis (Wang et al. 2021; the count is read from the compendium). The transmission rate from adults to larvae is illustrative. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} stage = BsalLarvalStage(:wang2021; adult_to_larva = 5.2) @printf("carry-over through metamorphosis: %.1f; R0 = %.1f\n", stage.carry_over, basic_reproduction_number(p, stage)) u3, t3 = lar(stage, T()), lar(stage, block; coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", "host", "+ larvae infected, carry-over 0.5", u3.mean_adults, t3.mean_adults, "small change at this carry-over") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` carry-over through metamorphosis: 0.5; R0 = 24.9 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (step = 3, untreated = 0.039, treated = 0.334) ``` ::: ::: This is the host model used for the rest of Part A. #### The host model in equations Densities are adult females and larvae per hectare; time is in years. Steps 0 and 1 use `ProbioticSLIProblem`, which has adults only. Step 1 is the model of Schmidt et al. (2017): $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS}{dt} &= b S - (d + \gamma N) S - \beta S I \\ \frac{dL}{dt} &= \beta S I - (d + e + \gamma N) L \\ \frac{dI}{dt} &= e L - (d + d_I + \gamma N) I \end{aligned} $$ with $N = S + L + I$ and $\gamma = (b - d)/K$, so that without Bsal $S$ settles at $K$. Only susceptible adults breed. Bsal enters as $I = 0.01$ per hectare (one per square kilometre) at $t = 0$. - **Step 0** is the same system with $e = 5000$ per year, so that $L$ empties within hours and the model is in effect $S \to I$. The printed $R_0 = \beta e K / ((b + e)(b + d_I))$, which tends to $\beta K / (b + d_I)$ as $e$ grows. - **Step 1** sets $e$ to its published value: a latent period of about one day. Steps 2 and 3 use `ProbioticLarvalProblem`, which adds uninfected and infected larvae, $W_S$ and $W_I$: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dW_S}{dt} &= b' S - (m + \mu_W) W_S - \beta_{WA} I W_S \\ \frac{dW_I}{dt} &= \beta_{WA} I W_S - (m + \mu_W) W_I \\ \frac{dS}{dt} &= m W_S + (1 - c)\, m W_I - (d + \gamma N) S - \beta S I \\ \frac{dL}{dt} &= c\, m W_I + \beta S I - (d + e + \gamma N) L \\ \frac{dI}{dt} &= e L - (d + d_I + \gamma N) I \end{aligned} $$ - **Step 2** replaces the recruitment term $b S$ in $dS/dt$ with births into the larval stage, $b' S$ with $b' = b (m + \mu_W)/m$. Larvae leave by metamorphosis at rate $m$ or die at rate $\mu_W$. The choice of $b'$ keeps the Bsal-free state of step 1 ($S = K$, plus $W_S = bK/m$ larvae). Here $\beta_{WA} = 0$ and $c = 0$, so $W_I$ stays at zero. - **Step 3** adds infection of larvae by infectious adults ($\beta_{WA} I W_S$) and carry-over: an infected larva becomes a latent adult with probability $c$, and a susceptible adult otherwise. Infected larvae do not die of Bsal and, in Part A, infect no one. (The code also has larva-to-larva and larva-to-adult transmission, `larva_to_larva` and `larva_to_adult`; both are zero throughout Part A.) The printed $R_0$ is the largest eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix for $(W_I, L, I)$ at the Bsal-free state. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ![The host model after step 3. Solid arrows are flows, labelled with the per-capita rate; dashed arrows show who breeds and who infects whom. Not drawn: every adult class also dies at rate d + γN and every larval class at the larval death rate.](01_building_realism_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: | Symbol | Meaning | Value or source | |---|---|---| | $S, L, I$ | susceptible, latent and infectious adults (per ha) | start at $S = K$ | | $W_S, W_I$ | uninfected and infected larvae (per ha) | start at $W_S = bK/m$ | | $b$ | recruitment rate | 0.39 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $d$ | natural death rate | 0.125 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $d_I$ | death rate from Bsal | 52 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $e$ | latent to infectious | 364 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017); 5000 in step 0 | | $\beta$ | transmission between adults | 52 ha per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $K$ | carrying capacity | 25 per ha, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $\gamma$ | density dependence | $(b - d)/K$ | | $m$ | metamorphosis rate, 1/larval period | 1/0.33 per yr, illustrative | | $\mu_W$ | larval death rate | 1 per yr, illustrative | | $b'$ | larvae born per susceptible adult | $b (m + \mu_W)/m$ | | $\beta_{WA}$ | transmission from adults to larvae | 0 in step 2; 5.2 ha per yr in step 3, illustrative | | $c$ | carry-over through metamorphosis | 0 in step 2; 0.5 in step 3, compendium (wang2021: 5 of 10 larvae) | The outcome is the mean of $(S + L + I)/K$ over the ten years after Bsal arrives. ### Treatment The reference treatment of step 3 is now made more realistic. Each step states what changed. #### The treatment in equations Every class is split into untreated ($U$) and treated ($T$). With all treatment terms present, the model of `ProbioticLarvalProblem` is, for adults, $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS_U}{dt} &= m\,[W_{SU} + (1 - r) W_{ST}] + (1 - c)\, m\,[W_{IU} + (1 - r) W_{IT}] \\ &\quad - (d + \gamma N) S_U - \lambda_A S_U + \omega S_T - a_A S_U \\ \frac{dS_T}{dt} &= r\, m W_{ST} + (1 - c)\, r\, m W_{IT} - (d + \gamma N) S_T - (1 - \varepsilon) \lambda_A S_T - \omega S_T + a_A S_U \\ \frac{dL_U}{dt} &= c\, m\,[W_{IU} + (1 - r) W_{IT}] + \lambda_A S_U - (d + e + \gamma N) L_U + \omega L_T - a_A L_U \\ \frac{dL_T}{dt} &= c\, r\, m W_{IT} + (1 - \varepsilon) \lambda_A S_T - (d + e + \gamma N) L_T - \omega L_T + a_A L_U \\ \frac{dI_U}{dt} &= e L_U - (d + d_I + \gamma N) I_U + \omega I_T - a_A I_U \\ \frac{dI_T}{dt} &= e L_T - (d + (1 - \tau) d_I + \gamma N) I_T - \omega I_T + a_A I_U \end{aligned} $$ and for larvae $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dW_{SU}}{dt} &= b'\,[S_U + S_T + \tau (L_T + I_T)] - (m + \mu_W) W_{SU} - \lambda_W W_{SU} + \omega W_{ST} - a_W W_{SU} \\ \frac{dW_{ST}}{dt} &= -(m + \mu_W) W_{ST} - (1 - \varepsilon) \lambda_W W_{ST} - \omega W_{ST} + a_W W_{SU} \\ \frac{dW_{IU}}{dt} &= \lambda_W W_{SU} - (m + \mu_W) W_{IU} + \omega W_{IT} - a_W W_{IU} \\ \frac{dW_{IT}}{dt} &= (1 - \varepsilon) \lambda_W W_{ST} - (m + \mu_W) W_{IT} - \omega W_{IT} + a_W W_{IU} \end{aligned} $$ with $N$ all adults and $$ \begin{aligned} \lambda_A &= \beta\,[I_U + (1 - \sigma) I_T], \qquad \lambda_W = \beta_{WA}\,[I_U + (1 - \sigma) I_T], \\ a_A &= \eta\, \frac{S_T + L_T + I_T}{N}, \qquad a_W = \eta\, \frac{W_{ST} + W_{IT}}{W_{SU} + W_{ST} + W_{IU} + W_{IT}}, \\ \omega &= \frac{\ln 2}{h}, \qquad (\varepsilon, \tau, \sigma) = g(t - t_k)\,(\varepsilon_0, \tau_0, \sigma_0), \qquad g(a) = \frac{1 + 1/F}{1 + 2^{a/h_B}/F}. \end{aligned} $$ Treatment itself is a pulse. At each treatment time $t_k$, a fraction $\phi$ (`coverage`) of every untreated class of the treated stage moves to the matching treated class, and the clock of $g$ restarts ($t_k$ is the most recent application). Bsal arrives just after any treatment at the same time. Recruits are born untreated. In steps 0 and 1 (`ProbioticSLIProblem`, no larvae) the adult equations are the same without the metamorphosis terms, and recruits $b\,[S_U + S_T + \tau (L_T + I_T)]$ enter $S_U$ directly. Treated, infected adults breed in proportion to $\tau$: this is an assumption of the code, and with $\tau = 0$ it is Schmidt's rule. (The code also has an environmental route of spread, `environmental`, and inheritance from treated mothers, `maternal`; both are zero throughout Part A and are left out above.) What each step switches on: - **Steps 0–3, reference treatment**: `efficacy = 0.99`, adults treated once at $t = 0$ with $\phi = 1$. So $\varepsilon_0 = 0.99$ and $\omega = \eta = \tau_0 = \sigma_0 = 0$, $g = 1$: treated adults are infected at 1% of the untreated rate, for life. - **Step 4**, `half_life = 1.0`: $\omega = \ln 2$ per year; treated animals revert to untreated. - **Step 5**, `direct = 50.0`: $\eta = 50$ per year. An untreated animal acquires the bacteria in proportion to the treated fraction of its own stage. The vignette prints the microbiome's reproduction number $R_m = \eta/(\omega + b)$, with adult turnover $b$, and the long-run coverage $1 - 1/R_m$. Larvae are never treated in this step, so recruits acquire the bacteria only from adults. - **Step 6**, `tolerance = 0.9` and no `efficacy`: $\varepsilon_0 = 0$, $\tau_0 = 0.9$. A treated, infected adult dies of Bsal at $(1 - \tau) d_I$, stays infectious, and breeds at $\tau$. The printed reproduction number, with all adults treated, is $R_0\,[1 - \phi + \phi M]$ with $M = (1 - \varepsilon)(1 - \sigma)(b + d_I)/(b + (1 - \tau) d_I)$. This uses the adults-only model and ignores gain or loss of the bacteria during an infection. - **Step 7**, `load_reducing_treatment` with reduction in load $\rho$ and `death_exponent` $k$: $\sigma_0 = \rho$ and $\tau_0 = 1 - (1 - \rho)^k$, with $\varepsilon_0 = 0$. The run uses $\rho = 0.99$, $k = 1$, so $\sigma_0 = \tau_0 = 0.99$; loss and spread as in step 5. - **Step 8**: the treatment of step 7, with `treat = :larvae` or `:both`, which applies the pulse to $W_{SU} \to W_{ST}$ and $W_{IU} \to W_{IT}$ as well, every quarter; `retention` is $r$. Treated larvae shed less, through $\sigma$ in $\lambda_A$ and $\lambda_W$; larvae do not die of Bsal, so tolerance does nothing for them. - **Step 9**, `abundance_half_life = 5/365`, `protective_fold = 100`, on top of step 8: $g$ is no longer 1. It multiplies $\varepsilon_0$, $\tau_0$ and $\sigma_0$ (here $\tau_0$ and $\sigma_0$), falls to one half about $\log_2 F$ abundance half-lives after each application, and is reset to 1 by the next. All treated animals share one clock. The loss of step 4 ($\omega$) and the spread of step 5 ($\eta$) stay. ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ![Treatment of adults. Blue boxes are treated animals. Solid arrows are flows with per-capita rates; dashed arrows feed the force of infection. Not drawn: background death d + γN of every class, and the pulses of treatment that move a fraction φ from each untreated class up to the treated one.](01_building_realism_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ![Treatment of larvae and what happens at metamorphosis. All larvae are born uninfected and untreated, to susceptible adults and, in proportion to τ, to treated infected adults. The force of infection on larvae has the same form as on adults, with the adult-to-larva rate in place of β. Not drawn: larval death.](01_building_realism_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: | Symbol | Meaning | Value or source | |---|---|---| | $U, T$ | untreated, treated | | | $\varepsilon_0$ | `efficacy`: reduction in the infection rate | 0.99 in steps 0–5; 0 from step 6; illustrative | | $\tau_0$ | `tolerance`: reduction in death from Bsal | 0.9 in step 6; 0.99 from step 7; illustrative | | $\sigma_0$ | `shedding_reduction`: reduction in shedding | 0.99 from step 7; illustrative | | $h$, $\omega$ | `half_life` of treatment and loss rate $\ln 2 / h$ | $h$ = 1 yr from step 4, before that none ($\omega = 0$); illustrative | | $\eta$ | `direct`: spread of the bacteria | 50 per yr from step 5, before that 0; illustrative | | $\phi$ | `coverage` at each treatment | 1 | | $t_k$ | `treat_times` | 0 in steps 0–7; every quarter from 0 to 9.75 yr in steps 8–9 (monthly in one run) | | $r$ | `retention` at metamorphosis | 0 or 1 in step 8, 1 in step 9; illustrative, not measured | | $h_B$ | `abundance_half_life` of the applied bacteria | 5 days in step 9, from this project's fits to Knapp et al. (2022) and Madison et al. (2025) | | $F$ | `protective_fold` | 100 in step 9 (10 and 1000 in the plot); illustrative, not measured | | $g$ | `protection`: share of the full effect left after time $a$ | 1 except in step 9 | #### Step 4. Protection is lost A treated animal reverts to untreated, with a half-life of one year. ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} a = lar(stage, T(efficacy = 0.99, half_life = 1.0); coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", "treatment", "+ protection lost, half-life 1 year", u3.mean_adults, a.mean_adults, "collapse only delayed") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (step = 4, untreated = 0.039, treated = 0.133) ``` ::: ::: #### Step 5. The bacteria spread between animals Treated animals pass the bacteria to others, so protection can reach the recruits. ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} spread = T(efficacy = 0.99, half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0) @printf("microbiome reproduction number %.0f, long-run coverage %.2f\n", microbiome_reproduction_number(spread; turnover = p.b), equilibrium_coverage(spread; turnover = p.b)) a = lar(stage, spread; coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", "treatment", "+ bacteria spread between animals", u3.mean_adults, a.mean_adults, "full protection: the microbiome maintains itself") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` microbiome reproduction number 46, long-run coverage 0.98 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (step = 5, untreated = 0.039, treated = 0.999) ``` ::: ::: A model stopped here says: **a self-spreading, strongly protective microbiome works, and nothing else does.** #### Step 6. What trials show: survival, not fewer infections In challenge trials, treated animals were infected as often as untreated ones, but fewer died. The compendium holds the counts from one trial in *Rana muscosa* (Harris et al. 2009): ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} h = parameter_set(:harris2009ismej) mortality_reduction(h.deaths_treated, h.n_treated, h.deaths_control, h.n_control; rng = Xoshiro(1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (median = 0.9528399509303813, lower = 0.5571631729768851, upper = 0.9998974605554769) ``` ::: ::: So the mechanism is changed: treatment reduces disease-induced death (`tolerance`) and does not block infection. A treated, infected animal stays infectious. Loss and spread are as in step 5. ::: {#28 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} tolerant = T(tolerance = 0.9, half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0) @printf("Bsal reproduction number if everyone is treated: %.0f (untreated %.0f)\n", effective_reproduction_number(p, tolerant, 1.0), basic_reproduction_number(p)) a = lar(stage, tolerant; coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", "treatment", "mechanism as in trials: survive, still infected", u3.mean_adults, a.mean_adults, "fails; survivors shed for longer, so transmission rises") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bsal reproduction number if everyone is treated: 232 (untreated 25) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (step = 6, untreated = 0.039, treated = 0.025) ``` ::: ::: #### Step 7. Lower load: less death and less shedding Bacteria that suppress the fungus should lower the load on the animal, and so reduce shedding as well as death. Both now follow from one reduction in load: shedding in proportion to load, death in proportion to load raised to a power `k`. ::: {#30 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} reductions = [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999] ks = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0] R = [effective_reproduction_number(p, load_reducing_treatment(ρ; death_exponent = k), 1.0) for ρ in reductions, k in ks] plot(string.(reductions), R; yscale = :log10, marker = :circle, xlabel = "reduction in load", ylabel = "Bsal reproduction number, all treated", label = permutedims(["k = $k" for k in ks]), legend = :topright) hline!([1.0]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "threshold") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: With death proportional to load (`k = 1`) the two effects nearly cancel: the animal sheds less but for longer. ::: {#32 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} a = lar(stage, load_reducing_treatment(0.99; half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0); coverage = 1.0) step!("Bsal", "treatment", "+ lower load (99%): also less shedding", u3.mean_adults, a.mean_adults, "partial; survivors remain infected") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (step = 7, untreated = 0.039, treated = 0.189) ``` ::: ::: #### Step 8. Treat larvae as well With larvae in the host model they can be treated too. Whether a treated larva keeps the bacteria through metamorphosis (`retention`) has not been measured. The pond model Mitchell's model is the simplest available for this system, though it is not as simple as step 0 of Part A: tadpoles are infected by zoospores in the pond, infected tadpoles are removed at metamorphosis, and juveniles and adults are never infected. The equations below are the host model as it stands after step 3. Time $t$ is in years and $T$ is the time of year. Between the yearly events, $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dP_X}{dt} &= -(\mu_P + \nu Z)\,P_X \\ \frac{dP_Y}{dt} &= \nu Z\,P_X - (\mu_P + \alpha_P)\,P_Y \\ \frac{dM}{dt} &= -(\mu_J + \varepsilon)\,M \\ \frac{dA_X}{dt} &= \varepsilon M \left(1 - \frac{A_X + A_Y}{K}\right) - \mu_A A_X - \chi(t)\,\nu_A Z A_X + \sigma_A A_Y \\ \frac{dA_Y}{dt} &= \chi(t)\,\nu_A Z A_X - (\mu_A + \alpha_A + \sigma_A)\,A_Y \\ \frac{dZ}{dt} &= \rho P_Y + \chi(t)\,\rho_A A_Y + \gamma Z e^{-\varphi Z} - \mu_Z Z \end{aligned} $$ where $\chi(t) = 1$ while adults are at the pond ($t_1 \le T < t_1 + d_A/365$) and 0 otherwise. Three events happen each year: $$ \begin{aligned} T = t_1 &: \quad P_X \leftarrow P_X + \iota\psi\,(A_X + A_Y) \\ T = t_2 &: \quad J_0 = P_X\,(1 - q + q\,s_J) + P_Y\,s_J, \qquad q = 1 - e^{-\nu Z d_J / 365}, \qquad P_X,\ P_Y \leftarrow 0 \\ \omega \text{ after } t_2 &: \quad M \leftarrow M + J_0\,e^{-\mu_J \omega} \end{aligned} $$ At breeding, tadpoles are born to every adult. At metamorphosis the tadpoles leave the pond as a juvenile cohort $J_0$; $Z$ in $q$ is its value at that moment. Bd in frogs The outcome in Part C is the **fraction of 80 frogs sharing one pool that are alive after two years**. Disease here depends on the fungal load on each frog. Treatment is introduced at step 3. ### Host and pathogen #### Step 0. Load on each frog In the model of Briggs et al. (2010) each frog carries a load of sporangia. Sporangia release zoospores into a shared pool, zoospores infect frogs, and a frog dies when its load reaches a lethal level. Loads run away when there are enough frogs to keep the pool topped up. The equations below are the model as it stands after step 2. Each live frog $i$ carries $S_i$ sporangia, and the pool holds $Z$ zoospores: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS_i}{dt} &= \frac{\nu\gamma}{V}\,Z + (\eta\nu f - \sigma)\,S_i - \frac{c_i\,S_i}{h + S_i}, \\ \frac{dZ}{dt} &= \varepsilon + \eta(1 - f)\sum_{j\ \mathrm{alive}} S_j - \mu Z - \frac{\gamma}{V}\,N_{\mathrm{alive}}\,Z. \end{aligned} $$ Zoospores meet each frog at rate $\gamma/V$, and a fraction $\nu$ of meetings start a sporangium. Each sporangium releases $\eta$ zoospores a day: a fraction $f$ reinfect the same frog and the rest go to the pool. A frog dies when $S_i$ reaches $S_{\max}$; from then on it sheds nothing and takes up no zoospores. All frogs start with no sporangia, and the pool starts at $\varepsilon/(\mu + \gamma N/V)$. On its own a frog's load would decline, because $\eta\nu f$ (about 0.04 per day) is below $\sigma$; loads run away only when enough frogs feed the pool. What each step adds: - **Step 0** is the model of Briggs et al. (2010) with no clearance ($c_i = 0$). The $S_i$ and $Z$ equations without $\varepsilon$ are those of the paper. The outside input $\varepsilon$ is the paper's external source of zoospores (its Fig. 3D), here as a constant rate. - **Step 1** adds clearance by the frog, $c\,S_i/(h + S_i)$, the same for every frog ($c_i = c$). at step 6, the effect seen in trials makes the same treatment fail; treating larvae as well (step 8) does not rescue it, although it would protect fully with bacteria that blocked infection; and at step 9 bacteria that last a few weeks fail whatever else is done. 2. **Host biology can move the answer as much as treatment biology, but not everywhere.** A larval stage changed the untreated fate of the salamanders. One survival probability for infected toad metamorphs reversed both the untreated outcome and the value of the reference treatment. The [second vignette](../02_nested_model/02_nested_model.md) tests this like for like in a single model and finds that it depends on the regime: for Bsal at the published host density, six pieces of host biology barely change the outcome, and near the invasion threshold they change it a great deal. Its stochastic version also shows that chance can matter more than any of them: with whole animals, blocking infection in every adult on arrival nearly always eliminates Bsal, where the equations of step 1 here leave about a third of the population. 3. **How protection works matters more than how strong it is, and its effect has no fixed sign.** Letting animals survive infection is the worst change for Bsal and an improvement for toads. 4. **Effects interact.** The factorial shows that the value of spread, of treating larvae or of a lasting treatment each depends on the other pieces. 5. **The systems differ for structural reasons.** A toad cohort passes through a short infected stage once a year and can be re-treated. A salamander must be protected for life against a pathogen that kills in a week. In frogs, where disease follows a load that builds slowly, short-lived bacteria can still work if they are re-applied. 6. **Chance is a piece of realism, and it changed the answer in every system, in different directions.** For Bsal it made the reference treatment, which blocks infection, protect nearly the whole population, because Bsal arriving among treated animals is lost before it can establish; it did not rescue the final treatment, which does not block infection. For toads it overturned the published extinction of both host and pathogen. For frogs it made treatment harder, because random high loads tip the population sooner. ## What is not in the models - In Parts A and B bacterial abundance is a clock since the last dose, not a state of each animal. Only the frog model of Part C tracks it per animal. - The fold-drop in abundance at which protection is lost has not been measured, nor has the effect of the bacteria on clearance, nor whether applied bacteria survive metamorphosis. - The Bsal model has no recovery from infection and no years between metamorphosis and maturity. The toad model has thresholds standing in for extinction, and adult toads are never treated. - The three systems do not share one model structure, so Part B starts from a more complex model than Part A. The [second vignette](../02_nested_model/02_nested_model.md) uses one nested model, for the salamander system, in which every piece of biology is a switch. - No fade-out rule is applied in Part A, so densities can fall to meaningless values and recover. The second vignette shows what such a rule changes. - The stochastic steps use one introduced infected animal (Part A) or the published introduction (Parts B and C), one population size, and time steps of hours to a day.
